items.name: Cable crossover
items.description: Two tall weight-stack towers joined by a frame, each with a pulley that slides from floor to overhead. The gym standard for cable flys, pushdowns, face pulls and almost any cable exercise.
items.weight_options: Two stacks of ~70–115 kg (150–250 lb) each, usually 1:1 or 2:1 cable ratio
items.adjustability: Pulleys adjust in 15–30 positions; most have a pull-up bar across the top.
items.buying_tips: Check the cable ratio: 2:1 stacks feel half as heavy and travel twice as far, so numbers are not comparable to 1:1 machines.
items.safety: Check cables for fraying and that the pin is fully seated before each set.

items.name: Functional trainer / cable column
items.description: A compact two-stack cable machine with swivelling arms that move up and down a column, letting you pull from any height and angle. The most popular cable unit for home gyms.
items.weight_options: Two 70–100 kg (150–220 lb) stacks, usually 2:1 ratio
items.adjustability: Arms adjust in height (and on some, pivot sideways); usually a top pull-up bar.
items.buying_tips: Look for smooth pulleys, enough cable travel for overhead work (check 2:1 travel length) and fine weight increments.
items.safety: Keep fingers away from the stack and moving pulleys.

items.name: Single-stack cable tower
items.description: One weight stack with a single pulley that slides along a vertical column. Does nearly every cable exercise one side at a time.
items.adjustability: Pulley adjusts in height; some rotate.
items.buying_tips: A good space-saver if you do not need two-handle flys; check the top pulley clears your height for pulldowns.
items.safety: Bolt or weight the base if the manual says so.

items.name: Wall-mounted cable pulley
items.description: A cable column or track bolted straight to a wall stud or masonry, with a stack or plate horn and a sliding pulley. Saves floor space compared with a tower.
items.weight_options: Stack 40–90 kg or plate horn loaded with plates
items.adjustability: Pulley slides on the track; some fold flat.
items.buying_tips: Make sure your wall can take the load; masonry or doubled studs are safest.
items.safety: Anchor into structural framing only.

items.name: Hi-lo pulley station
items.description: Commercial single stack with fixed high and low pulleys (or a short adjustable carriage), often placed at the end of a row of machines.
items.adjustability: Fixed or limited height positions.
items.buying_tips: Mainly a commercial purchase; homes are better served by an adjustable tower.

items.name: Lat pulldown machine
items.description: A seated station with thigh pads and an overhead pulley for pulling a bar down to the chest. The main way to train vertical pulling without doing pull-ups.
items.weight_options: Stack 80–130 kg (180–300 lb); home versions often plate loaded
items.adjustability: Adjustable knee pad; seat height on most.
items.buying_tips: Check the knee pad locks you down and that the stack is heavy enough as you get stronger.

items.name: Seated cable row
items.description: A low pulley with a bench and foot plate for seated horizontal rows. Found as a standalone station or as part of a lat/row combo.
items.adjustability: Fixed; some have adjustable foot plates or a chest pad.
items.buying_tips: Long rails need more floor length than people expect; measure first.

items.name: Lat pulldown / low row combo
items.description: One stack serving both a high pulley with knee pads for pulldowns and a low pulley with foot plate for rows. The standard home back station.
items.weight_options: Stack 90–110 kg (200–250 lb), or plate loaded
items.adjustability: Adjustable knee pad and seat; swap between pulleys.
items.buying_tips: Plate-loaded versions are cheaper and never run out of weight; stack versions change load faster.

items.name: Rack lat / low row attachment
items.description: A pulley system bolted onto a power rack (or the back of a bench) with a plate horn and seat or foot plate, adding pulldowns, low rows and pushdowns without a separate machine.
items.adjustability: Usually high and low pulleys; some add an adjustable seat.
items.buying_tips: Match the hole spacing and tube size to your rack brand.
items.safety: Make sure the rack is bolted down or heavy enough not to tip.

items.name: Rack-mounted cable arms
items.description: A pair of adjustable pulley carriages and stacks or plate horns that mount to the uprights of a power rack, turning it into a functional trainer.
items.weight_options: Plate horns or 70–90 kg stacks per side
items.adjustability: Pulleys slide on the rack uprights.
items.buying_tips: Plate-loaded kits are cheaper; check the cable ratio and that your rack is deep enough.

items.name: Plate-loaded cable tower
items.description: A freestanding cable tower or functional trainer with plate horns instead of a weight stack. Cheaper and lighter to ship than stack units.
items.adjustability: Adjustable pulley carriages; some have fixed high/low only.
items.buying_tips: Small plates (1.25–2.5 kg) matter more here because cable moves need small jumps.

items.name: Loading pin pulley (DIY cable)
items.description: A pulley wheel, steel cable and loading pin that clip onto a rack, pull-up bar or wall anchor. The cheapest way to do cable pushdowns, curls and pulldowns at home.
items.adjustability: Clip the pulley at any height on a rack or bar.
items.buying_tips: Pick a steel cable (not nylon cord) and ball-bearing pulleys; buy a long enough cable for overhead extensions.
items.safety: Inspect the cable and clips every session; keep your head out of the line of pull.

items.name: Multi-station cable jungle
items.description: A large commercial frame with 4–8 weight stacks around it: crossover, lat pulldown, low row and adjustable pulleys, plus a chin-up bar.
items.adjustability: Several adjustable and fixed pulleys.
items.buying_tips: Commercial only; needs ceiling height and a flat, strong floor.

items.name: Air-resistance cable trainer
items.description: A cable column whose resistance comes from compressed air instead of plates, so load changes by button and speed work is safe.
items.weight_options: Resistance adjusts in ~0.5 kg (1 lb) steps up to ~100 kg
items.adjustability: Push-button load; adjustable arms.
items.buying_tips: Needs an air compressor and is pricey; mostly seen in rehab and sport-performance gyms.

items.name: Flywheel (isoinertial) trainer
items.description: A strap wound around a spinning flywheel: you pull to spin it up and then brake it on the way back, giving hard eccentric overload. Used for squats, rows and sport training.
items.weight_options: Swappable flywheels set the inertia (resistance comes from flywheel inertia, not weights)
items.adjustability: Change flywheel discs or cone; harness or handle attaches to the strap.
items.buying_tips: Most used in sport and rehab; portable units exist but the platform type is the most versatile.
items.safety: Learn the timing on light flywheels first; the eccentric is much harder than it feels.

items.name: Smith machine
items.description: A barbell fixed in guide rails with hooks you twist to rack it at many heights. Lets you squat, press and lunge without a spotter, and doubles as a fixed bar for inverted rows.
items.weight_options: Bar 7–25 kg (counterbalanced bars feel lighter than their weight)
items.adjustability: Vertical or 5–7° angled rails; adjustable safety stops.
items.buying_tips: Ask what the bar weighs (or its counterbalance) so you can log real loads; linear-bearing rails glide best.
items.safety: Set the safety stops just below your lowest point every time.

items.name: 3D / multi-plane Smith machine
items.description: A Smith machine whose bar carriage also slides forward-back and side-to-side, so the bar path is guided vertically but free horizontally.
items.adjustability: Locks for the horizontal axes on some models.
items.buying_tips: Feels closer to a free bar than a standard Smith; good for gyms whose members fear free weights.
items.safety: Lock the horizontal axes until you are confident controlling the bar.

items.name: Smith attachment for power rack
items.description: A guided-rail bar kit that installs inside a power rack, adding Smith machine work without a separate machine.
items.adjustability: Rails bolt into the rack; bar hooks at many heights.
items.buying_tips: Only buy one made for your exact rack model and height.
items.safety: Recheck the bolts after the first few sessions.

items.name: Smith / functional trainer combo
items.description: A single frame combining a Smith machine, a power rack, dual adjustable cable pulleys, lat pulldown and low row, and a pull-up bar. Popular for complete home gyms.
items.weight_options: Two 70–100 kg stacks or plate horns; Smith bar 10–20 kg
items.adjustability: Adjustable pulleys, J-hooks, safeties and Smith hooks.
items.buying_tips: Check ceiling height, whether it includes a free-weight rack, and the cable ratio; stack versions cost more but change load quickly.
items.safety: Set Smith safeties before every set.
items.keywords: all in one smith cable combo

items.name: Home multi-gym
items.description: One frame with a weight stack and several stations: chest press, pec fly, lat pulldown, low row, leg extension and curl. Covers the basics in a small space.
items.adjustability: Adjustable seat, arms and pulleys; stations vary by model.
items.buying_tips: Look for a stack heavy enough for leg work and a low pulley; cheaper units have small stacks and jerky cables.

items.name: Plate-loaded leverage gym
items.description: A multi-gym that loads plates on lever arms instead of a stack, with press, row, pulldown and leg stations. Feels more like commercial plate-loaded machines.
items.adjustability: Adjustable seat and arm start positions.
items.buying_tips: Check the plate horn size (50 mm Olympic) and that the lever arms move independently if you want unilateral work.

items.name: Power rod / bow home gym
items.description: A compact home gym that uses bending rods instead of weights, with cables and a sliding bench for presses, rows, curls and leg work.
items.weight_options: Rods 5–200+ kg-equivalent; resistance rises as they bend
items.adjustability: Swap rods to change load; adjustable bench.
items.buying_tips: Rated loads are at full bend, so the real resistance is lower; good for beginners and tight budgets.

items.name: Incline bodyweight trainer
items.description: A sliding seat on an adjustable incline rail with cables: you pull or push yourself up the slope, so steeper angles mean more load. Folds flat for storage.
items.weight_options: Load is a share of bodyweight set by the incline
items.adjustability: Incline adjusts in 6–12 levels; some take add-on weight bars.
items.buying_tips: Check the user weight limit and how flat it folds.

items.name: Wall-mounted digital cable gym
items.description: A screen on the wall with two motor-driven cable arms that fold out. Motors create the resistance, so weight changes instantly, and it can add eccentric, chain or spotter modes.
items.adjustability: Arms swing and slide to any height; software modes.
items.buying_tips: Needs a subscription for full features and stud or masonry mounting; check max load suits your strength.
items.safety: Use the app or button to cut load if you fail a rep.

items.name: Freestanding digital home gym
items.description: A floor-standing unit with two motorised cable arms, a screen and usually a folding bench and bar. Rolls away when not in use.
items.adjustability: Arms adjust height and angle; bench folds.
items.buying_tips: Compare peak load, cable length and noise; check the warranty on the motors.

items.name: Portable digital cable trainer
items.description: A small motor box with one cable that anchors to the floor, a door, a rack or a wall. Gives cable training with app-set resistance anywhere.
items.weight_options: Up to ~25–100 kg (50–220 lb) depending on model
items.adjustability: Anchor at any height; modes for eccentric, isokinetic, chains.
items.buying_tips: Check what the anchor options are and whether the cable is long enough for overhead work.
items.safety: Make sure the anchor is rated above the maximum load.

items.name: Digital platform trainer
items.description: A floor platform with motor-driven cables coming up from the base. Ideal for squats, deadlifts, rows and curls with instant load changes and eccentric overload.
items.adjustability: Low pull only; app modes.
items.buying_tips: Only pulls from the floor, so pair with bands or a bar for pulldown-type moves.
items.safety: Stand centred so cables run vertically.

items.name: Tricep rope
items.description: A short thick rope with knotted or capped ends that clips to a cable. Used for pushdowns, face pulls, curls and cable crunches.
items.adjustability: Fixed.
items.buying_tips: A longer rope gives more range on face pulls and overhead extensions.

items.name: Double / long tricep rope
items.description: Two separate ropes or one extra-long rope on a single clip, letting the hands travel further apart for bigger range on face pulls and extensions.
items.adjustability: Fixed.
items.buying_tips: Nice upgrade if standard ropes feel short for your frame.

items.name: V-handle / close-grip row handle
items.description: A triangle-shaped handle with two parallel grips close together, used for seated rows and close-grip pulldowns.
items.adjustability: Fixed; some swivel.
items.buying_tips: Pick knurled or rubber grips that do not spin.
items.keywords: v handle double d close grip

items.name: Tricep V-bar
items.description: A short bar bent into a V that hangs from the cable, so the wrists stay angled during tricep pushdowns.
items.adjustability: Fixed; usually swivels.
items.buying_tips: A swivel hook keeps the bar from twisting.

items.name: Single D-handle
items.description: A one-hand grip on a ring that clips to a cable. The basic attachment for single-arm and two-handle cable work.
items.weight_options: Sold singly or in pairs; metal stirrup or fabric strap types
items.adjustability: Fixed; pro-style grips rotate or angle.
items.buying_tips: Buy a pair; rotating or soft-strap handles are kinder on wrists for flys and laterals.

items.name: Straight cable bar
items.description: A short straight bar (40–50 cm), often with a revolving sleeve, used for pushdowns, cable curls, straight-arm pulldowns and upright rows.
items.adjustability: Fixed or revolving.
items.buying_tips: A revolving bar turns freely in your hands and feels smoother on curls.

items.name: EZ cable bar
items.description: A short cambered bar for cable curls and pushdowns that puts the wrists in a slightly angled grip.
items.adjustability: Fixed or revolving.
items.buying_tips: Good if straight bars bother your wrists.

items.name: Long lat bar
items.description: A long bar (100–120 cm) with bent ends for wide-grip pulldowns and wide rows.
items.adjustability: Fixed; multi-grip versions have extra neutral handles.
items.buying_tips: Knurled grips and a swivel hook help; check it clears your rack or tower frame.
items.keywords: lat bar long bar wide grip

items.name: Wide row bar
items.description: A medium-length bar with angled ends designed for wide-grip seated rows, keeping the hands in a semi-pronated grip.
items.adjustability: Fixed.
items.buying_tips: Nice-to-have if you do a lot of upper-back rowing; a lat bar can stand in.

items.name: MAG / neutral-grip bar
items.description: Bars with parallel handles at a fixed width (close, medium or wide), giving a palms-facing grip for pulldowns and rows.
items.weight_options: Close, medium and wide widths; pronated and supinated versions
items.adjustability: Fixed widths; sold singly or as a set.
items.buying_tips: A medium-width neutral bar is the most useful single choice.

items.name: Ankle strap / cuff
items.description: A padded cuff with a D-ring that wraps around the ankle (or wrist) so you can clip a cable to your leg for kickbacks, abductions and leg curls.
items.adjustability: Velcro or buckle.
items.buying_tips: Get a padded, wide strap with a metal D-ring; a pair lets you switch sides quickly.
items.safety: Make sure the Velcro is fully closed before loading.

items.name: Cable hip belt
items.description: A padded hip belt with a ring that clips to a low pulley or loading pin, letting you do belt squats, hip-hinge pulls and marches on a cable.
items.adjustability: Adjustable waist.
items.buying_tips: A dip belt works too but a wide, padded belt is more comfortable for heavy loads.

items.name: Neck harness
items.description: A head strap with a chain that holds plates or clips to a low cable for neck extensions and flexion.
items.adjustability: Adjustable straps.
items.buying_tips: Start very light; neck work needs tiny increments.
items.safety: Use slow controlled reps and never jerk the load.

items.name: Loading pin
items.description: A short steel post with a base that holds plates and hangs from a cable or carabiner. The weight for DIY pulleys and also used for grip training.
items.adjustability: Fixed.
items.buying_tips: A longer pin holds more plates; choose a 50 mm (Olympic) post.
items.safety: Never stand under a hanging loaded pin.

items.name: Carabiners & cable extenders
items.description: Steel clips and short chains or straps used to swap attachments, shorten or lengthen cables, and link pulleys to anchors.
items.adjustability: Fixed.
items.buying_tips: Buy steel load-rated clips, not keyring-style ones.
items.safety: Only use clips rated well above the loads you lift.

items.name: Back extension / Roman chair
items.description: A 45-degree bench with hip pads and ankle rollers for back extensions, glute-focused extensions and side bends.
items.weight_options: Add plates, dumbbells or bands for load
items.adjustability: Adjustable hip pad height.
items.buying_tips: Make sure the hip pad adjusts so the top of it sits just below your hip crease.

items.name: 90-degree back extension bench
items.description: A flat (horizontal) back extension bench where the torso hangs straight down, giving the hardest top position compared with the 45-degree version.
items.adjustability: Pad height adjusts.
items.buying_tips: Less common for homes; a GHD does the same plus more.

items.name: Seated back extension machine
items.description: A seated selectorised machine where you push back against a pad behind the upper back to extend the spine.
items.adjustability: Adjustable seat and start position.
items.buying_tips: Mainly found in commercial gyms; homes are better off with a Roman chair.
items.safety: Use controlled reps through a pain-free range.

items.name: Reverse hyper
items.description: A high pad you lie face-down on while swinging a weighted pendulum (or strap) back behind you with the legs. Trains glutes and lower back with traction on the spine.
items.adjustability: Strap or roller; some have rack-mount versions.
items.buying_tips: Pendulum models are smoother than fixed-arm versions; check the pad height suits your leg length.
items.safety: Do not let the pendulum swing you; control the return.

items.name: Glute-ham developer (GHD)
items.description: A bench with a hip pad and a foot plate with ankle rollers. Used for glute-ham raises, GHD sit-ups, back and hip extensions, and assisted Nordics.
items.weight_options: Add plates or bands for load
items.adjustability: Adjustable foot plate distance and pad height.
items.buying_tips: A good GHD has a large footplate adjustment range and a stable, heavy base.
items.safety: Build up to GHD sit-ups slowly; they are very hard on the hip flexors at first.

items.name: Nordic curl bench
items.description: A padded kneeling bench with fixed ankle hooks for Nordic hamstring curls; some angle or add a reverse-Nordic setting.
items.adjustability: Some adjust the ankle hooks and angle.
items.buying_tips: Look for thick knee padding and an incline option to progress gradually.
items.safety: Start with partial range; Nordics cause major soreness at first.

items.name: Nordic curl strap
items.description: A padded ankle strap that anchors under a door, around a bench or to the floor so you can do Nordic curls without a partner.
items.adjustability: Adjustable strap length.
items.buying_tips: Check the anchor is rated for your bodyweight; door anchors need a solid door.
items.safety: Use a thick pad under the knees.

items.name: Hip thrust bench / box
items.description: A low, stable, padded box or bench at the right height for the upper back during hip thrusts, often with band pegs and a bar stop so it never slides.
items.adjustability: Some have adjustable height or band pegs.
items.buying_tips: Height and stability matter most; a padded edge saves your back.
items.safety: Use a bar pad and secure the bench against a wall or heavy object.

items.name: Sissy squat bench
items.description: A low frame with a calf pad and foot plate that locks the lower legs so you can lean back into a sissy squat for intense quad work.
items.adjustability: Adjustable calf pad.
items.buying_tips: Look for a wide base and adjustable roller so it fits your shin length.
items.safety: Build up slowly; knees take a lot of stress.

items.name: Captain's chair / knee raise station
items.description: An upright frame with a back pad and elbow pads where you support yourself on the forearms and raise your knees or legs.
items.weight_options: Add ankle weights or a dumbbell between the feet
items.adjustability: Fixed; often combined with dip handles.
items.buying_tips: Check the elbow pads are thick and the back pad tall enough for your height.

items.name: Power tower
items.description: A freestanding tower combining a pull-up bar, dip handles and a captain's chair knee-raise station, sometimes with push-up handles.
items.weight_options: Add a dip belt or vest
items.adjustability: Some adjust the pull-up bar height.
items.buying_tips: Cheaper towers wobble on kipping; look for a wide base and a weight rating well above your bodyweight.
items.safety: Do not kip on a lightweight tower.

items.name: Ab / decline sit-up bench
items.description: An angled bench with leg rollers to hook the feet for decline sit-ups and crunches, or handles for reverse leg raises. Usually adjustable in angle.
items.weight_options: Hold a plate or medicine ball for load
items.adjustability: Adjustable decline angle and roller height.
items.buying_tips: Check that the foot rollers fit tall users and the angle adjusts in several steps.

items.name: AbMat (ab sit-up pad)
items.description: A curved foam wedge placed under the lower back so crunches and butterfly sit-ups get a bigger range of motion.
items.adjustability: Fixed; some come with a tailbone pad.
items.buying_tips: Pick a firm, tall-enough wedge; the cheaper soft ones flatten quickly.

items.name: Sit-up bar (floor anchor)
items.description: A padded bar that suctions or clamps to the floor or under a door to hold the feet down for sit-ups.
items.adjustability: Adjustable height on some.
items.buying_tips: Suction versions need a smooth floor; clamp versions are more secure.

items.name: Ab coaster / knee glider
items.description: A curved rail with a kneeling carriage: you hold handles and pull your knees up the arc, a supported version of a hanging knee raise.
items.weight_options: Some take plates on the carriage
items.adjustability: Twist the carriage for obliques.
items.buying_tips: Commercial versions are much smoother than cheap home copies.

items.name: Ab rocker / crunch frame
items.description: A rocking frame or padded lounge chair that supports the head and guides the crunch path. Mainly for beginners.
items.adjustability: Some recline in several settings.
items.buying_tips: Adds little beyond a floor crunch for most people; useful if neck strain is the issue.
